title: On the Genealogy of Morals
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
openingText: 1. We are unknown to ourselves, we knowers, and there is good reason for it. We have never searched for ourselves — so how should we ever find ourselves? It has been said rightly: "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Our treasure is where the hives of our knowledge stand. We are always heading for those hives. As born creatures of flight and honey-gatherers of the spirit, we really care in our hearts about one thing only — to bring something "home to the hive!"
about:
Where do our moral values come from, and what are they worth? In On the Genealogy of Morals, Nietzsche examines the histories, drives and relations of power that he sees behind good, evil, guilt and bad conscience. His accounts are challenging hypotheses and polemical interpretations, rather than neutral historical reports.

Published in 1887, the book consists of a preface and three essays. The first distinguishes “good and bad” from “good and evil” and examines ressentiment as a force in the transformation of values. The second connects guilt with debt, punishment, memory and drives turned inward. The third asks how the ascetic ideal gives suffering meaning, and whether science’s unconditional will to truth remains attached to that ideal.

Nietzsche argues through linguistic comparisons, historical examples, psychological interpretations and direct attacks on his opponents. Follow both the reasoning and the rhetoric: what do his examples establish, what does he assume, and where does an account of a value’s possible origins become a judgment of its worth?

angleCards.title: Good and bad—or good and evil?
angleCards.text: The first essay presents two ways of creating values. Nietzsche’s noble type begins by affirming itself; slave morality begins by rejecting an enemy. Examine what that difference means and whether his examples support it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the distinction between “good and bad” and “good and evil” and examine the role of ressentiment.

angleCards.title: Guilt, debt and bad conscience
angleCards.text: The second essay connects German Schuld, guilt, with Schulden, debts. It also explores how restrained drives can turn against their owner. Keep these accounts distinct while following the connections Nietzsche makes between them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the links between debt, punishment, memory and bad conscience without taking the genealogy as already proved.

angleCards.title: What does the ascetic ideal do?
angleCards.text: The same ideal can mean different things for an artist, a philosopher and a priest. Follow those distinctions before assessing the claim that the ideal both opposes life and helps suffering people hold on to it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the different functions of the ascetic ideal and its connection to science’s will to truth.

angleCards.title: From origins to value
angleCards.text: The preface calls for a critique of the value of moral values themselves. Read with attention to the difference between explaining where a value comes from and deciding whether to retain it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine when Nietzsche’s historical and psychological explanations also justify his judgments.

cast.name: The Noble Type
cast.description: In the first essay, the noble type takes itself and its way of life as the standard of good. Its opposite is then called bad. This is a type within Nietzsche’s argument, not a single historical person.

cast.name: Slave Morality
cast.description: Nietzsche describes a way of valuing that first identifies an evil enemy and then defines itself as good. Ressentiment becomes a creative force in this account.

cast.name: Ressentiment
cast.description: A persistent, reactive resentment that cannot discharge itself directly in action. The concept connects the book’s inquiries into morality, revenge and the ascetic priest’s power.

cast.name: Bad Conscience
cast.description: In the second essay, Nietzsche explains bad conscience through drives that can no longer find free outward expression and therefore turn against their owner.

cast.name: The Ascetic Priest
cast.description: In the third essay, the priest gives suffering meaning by interpreting it as guilt. He protects his herd and binds it to life, while potentially intensifying its suffering.

cast.name: The Knower
cast.role: THE WILL TO TRUTH ALSO FACES SCRUTINY
cast.description: The book begins with knowers being unknown to themselves. Later, its critique turns toward the unconditional belief in truth’s value and therefore toward the inquirer’s own assumptions.

whyItMatters.title: Values acquire a history
whyItMatters.body: The book invites readers to investigate how values arise, whom they benefit and which ways of life they support. It provides a starting point for testing moral assumptions without confusing an explanation of their origins with a final judgment of their worth.

whyItMatters.title: Guilt becomes a question
whyItMatters.body: Nietzsche examines guilt as something with a history that admits different interpretations. The connections between debt, punishment and inward cruelty are arguments to examine, rather than diagnoses the reader must accept.

whyItMatters.title: Critique turns back on itself
whyItMatters.body: The third essay asks whether even those who reject religion can remain bound to an ascetic ideal through unconditional faith in truth. It challenges readers to examine the aims and assumptions of criticism itself.
